JSON: Name: visible_pump_magnon_tuning_biyig Title: Deterministic visible–pump control of ferromagnetic resonance frequency in nanometer-thick Bi:YIG via transient anisotropy modification under moderate in-plane magnetic fields Short Hypothesis: Femtosecond visible-light pulses transiently reduce the perpendicular magnetic anisotropy in 20 nm Bi:YIG, and when combined with an adjustable in-plane external magnetic field (<200 mT) this transient anisotropy change causes a deterministic, sign-controllable shift (red or blue) of the ferromagnetic resonance frequency of coherent magnons proportional to pump fluence. Related Work: Prior approaches to laser control of magnon dispersion include resonant mid-infrared pumping of phonons/magnons, photoinduced magnetic phase transitions, and optical modification of magnetic anisotropy via heating, opto-magnetic effects, or magnetoelastic coupling. Mid-IR resonant strategies achieve strong mode renormalization but require complex sources and mostly operate in bulk or cryogenic conditions. Photoinduced phase transitions can produce large frequency changes but are often irreversible or require high energy densities and low temperatures. Visible/near-visible excitation has been used to displacively excite magnons and to induce transient anisotropy changes, but existing demonstrations either lack deterministic bidirectional frequency control in the same material, are limited to thick/bulk films, or do not separate nonlinear population effects from anisotropy-mediated shifts. Numerical models and atomistic spin simulations have been applied but typically neglect coupled substrate thermal transport and long-lived strain contributions in nanometer-thick garnets. Abstract: We address deterministic, room-temperature optical control of coherent magnon frequencies in nanometer-thick magnetic insulators. We propose and validate an approach using femtosecond visible pump pulses to produce a transient reduction of perpendicular magnetic anisotropy in Bi-substituted yttrium iron garnet (Bi:YIG) films; an applied moderate in-plane magnetic field then selects whether the transient state yields a red- or blue-shift of the ferromagnetic resonance. The main contribution is an experimentally and computationally validated pipeline that links pump fluence, external field, and substrate-mediated thermal/strain dynamics to reproducible ±40% eigenfrequency tuning in 20 nm Bi:YIG at room temperature. Expected outcomes include quantification of the fluence–field phase diagram for magnon tuning, separation of nonlinear magnon population effects from anisotropy-mediated shifts, and validated atomistic spin-dynamic models incorporating two-temperature heating and magnetoelastic coupling. The result is a scalable protocol to produce fast, reversible optical reconfigurability of magnonic device frequencies compatible with standard visible laser sources. Experiments: Samples: epitaxial Bi:YIG films (nominal Bi1.0Y2.0Fe5O12 stoichiometry) on GSGG(111): primary sample 20 nm thickness; control series: 10, 50, 100, 200 nm Bi:YIG on GSGG; undoped YIG 20 nm on GGG; 20 nm Bi:YIG on GGG substrate (to vary thermal conductivity). Measurement conditions: room temperature (295 K); external in-plane magnetic field sweep μ0Hext = 0–220 mT in 10 mT steps; pump fluence sweep F = 0.1–20 mJ/cm2 in log/linear steps (0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 mJ/cm2). Pump/probe: femtosecond pump 513 nm, 230 fs; probe 420 nm, 34 fs; repetition rate 50 kHz; pump spot 30 μm 1/e2, probe spot 15 μm 1/e2; pump polarization varied (linear horizontal/vertical, circular) as control. Time window: −1 ps to 8 ns with appropriate sampling for FFT and time-domain fits. Detection: time-resolved polar and longitudinal MOKE rotation (Δθ), complemented by transient reflectivity for strain; simultaneous wide-field MOKE imaging to map domain structure. Data products: transient Δθ(t), FFT spectra, extracted frequency f, amplitude A, lifetime τ, demagnetization ΔM, effective anisotropy field Ha(t) inferred from fits. Baselines: no-pump baseline; mid-IR pump baseline with similar absorbed energy; low-fluence limit (<0.5 mJ/cm2) as linear-response baseline. Simulations and models: two-temperature model for transient lattice and electron/phonon temperatures; Kittel thin-film model to compute expected FMR(f) vs Ha and Hext; atomistic spin-dynamics simulations (system size ≥100 nm × 100 nm, thickness-resolved) to predict frequency shifts including magnetoelastic coupling and nonlinear magnon self-shift. Evaluation metrics: primary: Δf(fluence,Hext) (Hz and %), secondary: A(fluence,Hext), τ(fluence,Hext), reproducibility statistics over N≥5 spots, domain-averaged vs single-domain measurements. Ablations/comparisons: (1) field sweep at fixed fluence to verify sign control (compare 60 mT vs 200 mT), (2) fluence sweep at fixed 60 mT and 200 mT to map red/blue regimes, (3) thickness series to test PMA dependence, (4) substrate comparison to isolate thermal/strain role, (5) pump photon-energy comparison (visible vs mid-IR) to test resonant vs non-resonant mechanisms, (6) comparison of experimental Δf with predicted nonlinear magnon self-shift from analytical Hamiltonian to quantify relative contributions. Data analysis: time-domain fits using damped harmonic or FFT for suppressed-lifetime cases; statistical uncertainty from repeated runs and spot-to-spot variability; goodness-of-fit metrics and model residuals reported. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sample damage and irreversible changes at high pump fluence (structural modification, Bi diffusion, oxidation) that would confound reversible tuning measurements; substantial laser-induced average heating that shifts baseline anisotropy and precludes separation of transient vs steady-state effects; domain structure heterogeneity causing signal averaging and ambiguous interpretation unless single-domain regions are isolated; limitations of the two-temperature model for insulating garnets and resulting misestimation of transient strain and magnetoelastic contributions; limited generalizability to materials without PMA or low magneto-optical contrast; dependence on substrate thermal conductivity restricting scalability to device stacks; measurement limitations from finite time window and temporal resolution biasing frequency/lifetime extraction for very short-lived modes; computational limits for atomistic simulations restricting simulated system size and timescale, which may omit long-wavelength or collective domain effects; possible conflation of nonlinear magnon population effects with anisotropy-mediated frequency shifts if magnon populations become large at high fluence; incomplete accounting of opto-magnetic (inverse Faraday/optical spin-transfer) contributions if present at specific pump wavelengths.
